C09-M01-L03-F1.title: The RFC 3227 example order of volatility
C09-M01-L03-F1.caption: Seven layers from most volatile (top) to least volatile (bottom); everything above Disk exists only while the system runs.
C09-M01-L03-F1.alt: Stack of seven layers, most volatile at the top. Registers, cache: nanoseconds, rarely collectable (red). Routing, ARP, process table, kernel stats, memory: lost at power-off, live collection (red). Temporary file systems: tmpfs, /tmp, /dev/shm (orange). Disk: survives reboot, image it (blue). Remote logging and monitoring: SIEM, syslog, EDR, cloud audit (violet). Physical configuration, topology: cabling, ports, VLANs (slate). Archival media: backups, tapes, snapshots (green).

layers.label: Routing, ARP, process table, kernel stats, memory

C09-M01-L03-F2.title: Handling a running machine: what each option keeps and loses
C09-M01-L03-F2.caption: Five options compared by memory, disk and encryption state, with the main risk each one carries.
C09-M01-L03-F2.alt: Table with columns Option, Memory, Disk, Encryption, Main risk. Keep running and isolate (orange): kept; keeps changing; stays open; attacker notices or deadman switch. Capture memory, then decide (green): captured; small tool footprint; key likely in capture; footprint must be recorded. Graceful shutdown (red): lost; OS writes on the way down; locked; shutdown scripts destroy evidence. Hard power-off (red): lost; frozen at last write; locked; cached writes lost. Hibernate (orange): written to hiberfile; part overwritten by hiberfile; locked at rest; depends on resume.
rows: OS writes on the way down
C09-M01-L03-F2.note: No option leaves every layer untouched; record what was given up and why.
